name: ports
description: List the TCP ports that programs in the terminal are listening on, such as a development server's, with each port's address and the process that holds it. status is 'partial' when some processes couldn't be looked at, so a port missing from a partial reply may still be open. A truncated reply has an id, and blob_read with that id returns the whole list. It doesn't wake an idle terminal. To follow changes, call it once and then follow the ports_changed event.

status.description: How complete ports is: 'ok' if every process in the terminal was looked at, 'partial' if some could not be, so ports may be missing some, or 'unsupported' if this server cannot list ports for this terminal. Treat any other value as 'partial'.

address.description: The address the socket is bound to, as an IP literal with no brackets, such as 127.0.0.1, ::1, 0.0.0.0, or ::. An IPv4 address mapped into IPv6 is given as plain IPv4. An IPv6 link-local address keeps its zone, an interface index, as in fe80::1%1.

protocol.description: The transport protocol, 'tcp' today. Skip an entry whose protocol you don't know.

first_seen_at.description: When the server first saw this address and port held by this process in this terminal, as an RFC 3339 timestamp. The server looks in the background, every second while there is output or input in any terminal and every 5 minutes at most while nothing happens, and also when asked, so this can be minutes after the port opened. It changes if the port closes and opens again or another process holds it.

pid.description: The ID of the process that holds the socket, or the first started of several that share it. The process is described by the entry in processes with the same pid. Left out when the server can't tell which process holds the socket, such as a server started with sudo, and the reply is then partial.

ports.description: The ports that programs in the terminal listen on, sorted by port and then by address, with one entry for each protocol, address and port. An empty array when nothing is listening.

user_id.description: The user ID the process runs as on Unix, which shows when a command runs as another user, such as with sudo. Zero on Windows.

user.description: The name of the account the process runs as. Left out if it can't be looked up.

name.description: The file name of the executable, such as zsh. When path is left out, the system's own name for the process, which Linux limits to 15 bytes. To label a process, use the first of script, argv0, and name that is present.

path.description: The absolute path of the executable, with symlinks resolved. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process on Linux.

invoked_path.description: The absolute path the executable was started through, before symlinks were resolved, such as a link in a bin directory. Present only when Rex can confirm it leads to the same file as path.

argv0.description: The first argument as the process shows it now, such as -zsh for a login shell, cut to 256 bytes. Rex never returns the other arguments, because they can hold secrets.

script.description: For an interpreter such as node or python, the absolute path of the script it is running, as the user named it. Left out for other programs.

cwd.description: The process's working directory, as an absolute path. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process.

processes.description: The processes that hold the ports, sorted by pid, with one entry for each, described as the process method describes them. A pid in ports with no entry here is a process the server couldn't describe. Each is described when its first port is found, so fields such as cwd show their value from then.

truncated.description: True if entries were left out from the end of ports so that the reply fits in one message. processes then describes only the processes that the remaining entries name. Left out when false.

id.description: Set only when truncated is true. Names a stored copy of the whole reply, from the same scan. Read it with blob_read from offset 0 until eof, and decode the text as a ports reply. The server keeps it for a few minutes. Left out if the server couldn't store the copy.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.ports` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.
